The metal-to-metal clearances of a steam turbine are among the main drivers of efficiency.
The requirement to add clearances is driven by a number of factors, including relative movements of the steam turbine shell and rotor during transient conditions.
The installation of electric blankets on the outside of the steam turbine shell has been reported in many combined cycle and solar thermal units.
The main purpose of these installations is to keep the turbine warm during shutdown periods.
The proposed method is tolerant of changes in heat loss characteristics and simultaneous component failures.
The system uses external heating blankets to control temperature differentials between the shell halves.
The thermal model of the steam turbine shell is represented by a finite difference model with a total of N elements.
Each shell half is discretized into a total of 10 elements.
The heating blankets can be modeled as lumped thermal masses with electrical heaters embedded in them.
The generation of heat is assumed to be instantaneous.
The contact resistance between the heating blankets and the shell is challenging to determine due to installation variations.
The overall control system is required to be relatively insensitive to external installation variations.
The rotor can be modeled in a lumped parameter fashion as a single node.
The prediction of the rotor temperature is critical for the proper budgeting and management of low-cycle fatigue.
The deflection model described in Section III-B is used to estimate the current deflection profile of the shell.
The feedback gain matrix, K, is configured as a scalar matrix with all diagonal values equal to 50.
The outer loop of the controller is used to estimate the current deflection profile of the shell using the deflection model described in Section III-B.
The simulation results shown elsewhere in this study were obtained with 5 beam elements.
